summary: Defines a URI scheme for the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP), so a TFTP file can be named in link form, and discusses where the protocol is actually applicable. The authors discourage continued use of TFTP, largely because of security concerns, but acknowledge it has been used for a long time.

plainLanguage.summary: TFTP is a very simple way for computers to hand each other files, with almost no safety checks. This document gives it a web-style address format, but also warns people to be careful and avoid it when they can.

questions: what transfer modes does tftp support
subtitle: A web-style address format for the simple file transfer protocol.

tldr.problem: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) has been used for decades to transfer files between systems, but it lacked a standardized URI format that would fit modern conventions.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a URI scheme for TFTP following the pattern tftp://host/file with an optional mode parameter (netascii or octet), allowing files to be referenced and transferred using standard URI syntax.
tldr.outcome: Tools can now reference TFTP files using familiar URI notation, but the authors explicitly discourage TFTP use due to its many security and reliability limitations, recommending FTP or HTTP instead.

today: RFC 3617 is an Informational RFC that defined the TFTP URI scheme. TFTP itself remains a Standard Internet Protocol (STD 33), but this RFC explicitly recommends against its use in favor of FTP or HTTP for new applications. It survives primarily in legacy device bootstrapping scenarios.

sections.title: Introduction to TFTP
sections.content:
The Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a very simple protocol that has been in use on the Internet for a long time. Its primary uses have been to initially configure devices or to load new versions of operating system code onto network equipment. As modern systems adopted Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) and Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), a standardized way to reference TFTP files became desirable for completeness.

However, the authors of this RFC emphasize that they strongly recommend against the continued use of TFTP, largely due to security concerns. The definition of a URI provides tools with a standard namespace and structure, and it is hoped that this URI definition will ease transition from TFTP to modern file transfer mechanisms like FTP or HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP is used to quickly send files between computers, especially old network devices. This document creates an address format for it like you see on websites, but says 'don't use this old method anymore if you can help it'.

sections.title: TFTP URI Syntax
sections.content:
A TFTP URI follows the syntax tftp://host/file[;mode=...]. The scheme is always tftp://, followed by the host (which can be a domain name or IPv6 address in bracket notation per RFC 2732). The path is the file on the TFTP server, which may contain any ASCII characters with proper URI encoding.

The optional mode parameter specifies the transfer mode. The two modern modes are netascii (for text files) and octet (for binary data). If no mode is specified, octet mode is assumed. An obsolete mail mode was deprecated in RFC 1350 and is not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: A TFTP address looks like tftp://server.com/filename. You can add ;mode=netascii for text or ;mode=octet for binary, but octet is the default.

sections.title: Read and Write Operations
sections.content:
A TFTP URI can be used to reference a file that is to be found or placed on a TFTP server. When a TFTP URI is read, the underlying mechanism retrieves the named file from the specified host using the optionally specified mode. When a TFTP URI is written, the underlying mechanism transmits a file to a specified server at the given file path using the optionally specified mode. No other operations such as listing directories or changing permissions are supported.

Importantly, it is not possible to retrieve file size information prior to retrieval, nor can you determine file existence or permissions before transfer begins. Files transferred may or may not arrive intact, as there is no guarantee of reliability or completeness.
sections.plainLanguage: You can download a file from a TFTP server or upload one to it. But the protocol won't tell you if the file actually got there completely, or how big it is before you start.

sections.title: Security Concerns and Limitations
sections.content:
TFTP has multiple significant security and operational limitations. It offers no mechanism for access control and provides no protection against man-in-the-middle attacks. It relies on simple timeout mechanisms with no sophisticated congestion control. It cannot determine file sizes in advance, so implementations must carefully check transfer bounds to avoid exceeding memory or disk limitations.

TFTP is poorly suited to large files because there is no inherent integrity check or way to verify what was sent matches what was received. There is no way to restart transfers from anywhere except the beginning. TFTP is a strict lock-step protocol where only one packet can be in flight at a time. It offers no caching semantics and cannot work reliably across administrative domain boundaries due to UDP reliance and NAT/firewall issues. The authors strongly discourage use of TFTP except in the most limited circumstances where memory and CPU are at the highest premium.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP has no password protection, no way to check if a file got corrupted, and breaks if the network stutters. If you need to reliably move files, use FTP or HTTP instead.

sections.title: When TFTP Is Still Used
sections.content:
Despite its limitations, TFTP remains in use in specific scenarios where memory and processing power are severely constrained. Historical uses include bootstrapping network devices during installation and loading firmware onto embedded systems such as routers, switches, and other network appliances. In these narrow contexts, TFTP's simplicity has value because the application environment cannot support a more robust file transfer mechanism.

For any new applications or where more capable hardware exists, modern alternatives like HTTP or FTP provide superior reliability, security, and functionality. The URI definition in this RFC is primarily intended to provide a standard format for legacy systems that still depend on TFTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Very old or simple devices with tiny memory might still use TFTP to get their operating system when they first start up. Everything else should use a better method.
